Average enough independent draws from *almost* any distribution and that average is normally distributed — no matter how un-bell-shaped the thing you started with. Pick a base distribution, choose how many draws go into each average ($n$), and watch the histogram of many such averages settle onto the normal curve. Everything is drawn in **standardized units** $(\bar x - \mu)\sqrt{n}/\sigma$, so at $n = 1$ the histogram *is* the base distribution and the only thing that changes as you raise $n$ is its shape.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
```
```{ojs}
// URL preset helpers for the "Try an example" dropdown and shareable links.
// Supported query parameters:
//   dist   base distribution slug (one of VM.distributionOrder)
//   num    how many sample means to simulate (the histogram's sample size)
//   seed   RNG seed for the draws (reproducible)
//   n      draws averaged into each sample mean
//   bins   histogram bin count
//   show   comma-separated traces: hist, normal, base
urlParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)

maxN = 100

traceOptions = ["Sample-mean histogram", "Normal N(0, 1)", "Base distribution (n = 1)"]

// Matches the colors mainPlot uses for each trace, so the overlay legend's
// swatches double as a color key.
traceColors = new Map([
  ["Sample-mean histogram", "#2563eb"],
  ["Normal N(0, 1)", "#dc2626"],
  ["Base distribution (n = 1)", "#9ca3af"]
])

showSlugToLabel = new Map([
  ["hist", "Sample-mean histogram"],
  ["histogram", "Sample-mean histogram"],
  ["normal", "Normal N(0, 1)"],
  ["gaussian", "Normal N(0, 1)"],
  ["base", "Base distribution (n = 1)"],
  ["n1", "Base distribution (n = 1)"]
])

showLabelToSlug = new Map([
  ["Sample-mean histogram", "hist"],
  ["Normal N(0, 1)", "normal"],
  ["Base distribution (n = 1)", "base"]
])

initialDist = {
  const raw = urlParams.get("dist")
  if (raw !== null && VM.distributions[raw]) return raw
  return "exponential"
}

initialNum = urlParams.get("num") ?? "3000"

initialSeed = urlParams.get("seed") ?? "1"

initialN = {
  const raw = Number.parseInt(urlParams.get("n"), 10)
  if (Number.isInteger(raw) && raw >= 1 && raw <= maxN) return raw
  return 8
}

initialBins = {
  const raw = Number.parseInt(urlParams.get("bins"), 10)
  if (Number.isInteger(raw) && raw >= 12 && raw <= 60) return raw
  return 34
}

initialShow = {
  const raw = urlParams.get("show")
  if (raw === null || raw.trim() === "") return traceOptions
  const selected = []
  for (const piece of raw.split(",")) {
    const label = showSlugToLabel.get(piece.trim().toLowerCase())
    if (label && !selected.includes(label)) selected.push(label)
  }
  return selected.length > 0 ? selected : traceOptions
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Plain CSS selectors, not direct viewof references -- see
// js/ui/apply-example.js's comment for why (a cell that references a view
// by name becomes reactive on it, and since applying an example is what

exampleFieldSelectors = ({
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Applies the selected example's params to the fields above (including the
// sliders overlaid on the chart) and clicks Resample, in place -- no page
// reload, so no scroll jump. A plain "change" listener attached once to the
// stable native <select> (not an OJS cell reactive on exampleSelect's
// value): a <select> fires both "input" and "change" per selection, and a
// reactive cell would run once per event, with two overlapping calls
// racing.
applyExampleFromSelect = {
  const nativeSelect = (viewof exampleSelect).querySelector("select")
  if (!nativeSelect) return
  nativeSelect.addEventListener("change", () => {
    const example = (viewof exampleSelect).value
    if (!example) return
    VM.ui.applyExampleParams(exampleFieldSelectors, example.params, viewof resampleTrigger)
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Pressing Enter in the num/seed fields clicks Resample instead of
// submitting the field's own (invisible) form.
enterToResample = {
  for (const view of [viewof numInput, viewof seedInput]) {
    const input = view.querySelector("input")
    if (!input) continue
    input.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
      if (e.key !== "Enter") return
      e.preventDefault()
      viewof resampleTrigger.querySelector("button").click()
    })
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// committed snapshots the base distribution / count / seed fields only when
// Resample is clicked (it reads the stable `viewof` DOM nodes, not the
// reactive values, so it does not rerun on every keystroke) and writes them
// back into the URL. It deliberately does NOT read the live n / bins /
// trace-visibility controls -- those would make it reactive on them, so
// every slider tick would return a fresh object and force basePool to
// redraw the whole sample. urlSyncControls below keeps that trio in the URL
// instead. committed still runs once on initial load, so the first render
// honours a URL-provided (or default) setup with no click.
committed = {
  resampleTrigger
  const math = window.math

  const distVal = (viewof distSelect).value
  const numRaw = VM.expressions.makeNumber(math, (viewof numInput).value)
  const seedRaw = VM.expressions.makeNumber(math, (viewof seedInput).value)

  let M = 3000
  if (numRaw !== null && Number.isFinite(numRaw)) M = Math.round(numRaw)
  if (M < 400) M = 400
  if (M > 20000) M = 20000

  let seed = 1
  if (seedRaw !== null && Number.isFinite(seedRaw)) seed = Math.max(0, Math.floor(seedRaw))

  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  params.set("dist", distVal)
  params.set("num", (viewof numInput).value)
  params.set("seed", (viewof seedInput).value)
  history.replaceState(null, "", `${window.location.pathname}?${params}`)

  return {dist: distVal, M, seed}
}
```

```{ojs}
urlSyncControls = {

  params.set("n", String(n))
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// basePool draws committed.M independent groups of maxN raw base-distribution
// samples, once per Resample. `result` below averages the first n of each
// group -- so raising n folds in more of the SAME draws rather than
// reshuffling, which is what makes the histogram evolve smoothly as the
// slider moves (same trick as the noise slider on Polynomial Fits and the
// spread slider on K-Means).
basePool = {
  const dist = VM.distributions[committed.dist]
  const M = committed.M
  const rng = VM.sampling.seededRandom((Math.imul(committed.seed, 2654435761) + 12345) >>> 0)

  const pool = new Float64Array(M * maxN)
  for (let g = 0; g < M; g++) {
    const base = g * maxN
    for (let i = 0; i < maxN; i++) pool[base + i] = dist.sample(rng)
  }
  return {pool, M, dist}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// standardizedSampleMeans: for each of the M groups, the mean of its first
// `count` draws, standardized to (mean - mu) * sqrt(count) / sigma using the
// distribution's ANALYTIC mean and variance -- so at large count these land
// on N(0, 1) exactly, not merely on the empirical spread.
standardizedSampleMeans = (pool, M, dist, count) => {
  const mu = dist.mean
  const sigma = Math.sqrt(dist.variance)
  const zs = new Array(M)
  for (let g = 0; g < M; g++) {
    const base = g * maxN
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) sum += pool[base + i]
    zs[g] = (sum / count - mu) * Math.sqrt(count) / sigma
  }
  return zs
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// result: the standardized sample means at the current n, plus the
// standardized single draws (the n = 1 base-distribution reference).
result = {
  const {pool, M, dist} = basePool
  const zMeans = standardizedSampleMeans(pool, M, dist, n)

  const mu = dist.mean
  const sigma = Math.sqrt(dist.variance)
  const zBase = new Array(M)
  for (let g = 0; g < M; g++) zBase[g] = (pool[g * maxN] - mu) / sigma

  return {zMeans, zBase, M, n}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
sweepNs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 100]
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// sweep: how non-normal the sample-mean distribution still is at a ladder
// of sample sizes -- computed once per Resample (it does not depend on the
// live n slider), so the convergence plot and table below stay put while
// you scrub n. skewness and excess kurtosis of the mean of n i.i.d. draws
// are exactly gamma1/sqrt(n) and gamma2/n; the plot overlays those.
sweep = {
  const {pool, M, dist} = basePool
  const rows = []
  for (const count of sweepNs) {
    const zs = standardizedSampleMeans(pool, M, dist, count)
    const m = standardMomentSummary(zs)
    rows.push({
      n: count,
      mean: m.mean,
      sd: m.sd,
      skewness: m.skewness,
      excessKurtosis: m.excessKurtosis,
      ks: ksDistanceToNormal(zs)
    })
  }
  return rows
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
```
```{ojs}
// standardMomentSummary: mean, standard deviation, skewness, and excess
// kurtosis of an array, computed directly from central moments.
standardMomentSummary = (values) => {
  const count = values.length
  let sum = 0
  for (const v of values) sum += v
  const mean = sum / count

  let m2 = 0, m3 = 0, m4 = 0
  for (const v of values) {
    const d = v - mean
    const d2 = d * d
    m2 += d2
    m3 += d2 * d
    m4 += d2 * d2
  }
  m2 /= count
  m3 /= count
  m4 /= count

  const sd = Math.sqrt(m2)
  return {mean, sd, skewness: m3 / (sd * sd * sd), excessKurtosis: m4 / (m2 * m2) - 3}
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// erf: Abramowitz & Stegun 7.1.26 rational approximation (|error| < 1.5e-7),
// enough for a Kolmogorov-Smirnov readout.
erf = (x) => {
  let sign = 1
  if (x < 0) sign = -1
  const ax = Math.abs(x)
  const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * ax)
  const poly = ((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t
  return sign * (1 - poly * Math.exp(-ax * ax))
}

normalCdf = (z) => 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / Math.SQRT2))

normalPdf = (x) => Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// normalQuantile: Acklam's rational approximation to the standard-normal
// inverse CDF, for the QQ-plot's theoretical quantiles.
normalQuantile = (p) => {
  if (p <= 0) return -Infinity
  if (p >= 1) return Infinity

  const a = [-3.969683028665376e+01, 2.209460984245205e+02, -2.759285104469687e+02, 1.383577518672690e+02, -3.066479806614716e+01, 2.506628277459239e+00]
  const b = [-5.447609879822406e+01, 1.615858368580409e+02, -1.556989798598866e+02, 6.680131188771972e+01, -1.328068155288572e+01]
  const c = [-7.784894002430293e-03, -3.223964580411365e-01, -2.400758277161838e+00, -2.549732539343734e+00, 4.374664141464968e+00, 2.938163982698783e+00]
  const d = [7.784695709041462e-03, 3.224671290700398e-01, 2.445134137142996e+00, 3.754408661907416e+00]
  const plow = 0.02425
  const phigh = 1 - plow

  if (p < plow) {
    const q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(p))
    return (((((c[0] * q + c[1]) * q + c[2]) * q + c[3]) * q + c[4]) * q + c[5]) /
      ((((d[0] * q + d[1]) * q + d[2]) * q + d[3]) * q + 1)
  }
  if (p <= phigh) {
    const q = p - 0.5
    const r = q * q
    return (((((a[0] * r + a[1]) * r + a[2]) * r + a[3]) * r + a[4]) * r + a[5]) * q /
      (((((b[0] * r + b[1]) * r + b[2]) * r + b[3]) * r + b[4]) * r + 1)
  }
  const q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - p))
  return -(((((c[0] * q + c[1]) * q + c[2]) * q + c[3]) * q + c[4]) * q + c[5]) /
    ((((d[0] * q + d[1]) * q + d[2]) * q + d[3]) * q + 1)
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// ksDistanceToNormal: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic sup_x |F_n(x) - Phi(x)|
// between the empirical CDF of `values` and the standard normal.
ksDistanceToNormal = (values) => {
  const sorted = values.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b)
  const count = sorted.length
  let d = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    const cdf = normalCdf(sorted[i])
    const above = (i + 1) / count - cdf
    const below = cdf - i / count
    if (above > d) d = above
    if (below > d) d = below
  }
  return d
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// setup: bins the standardized sample means (and the n = 1 reference) into
// density histograms over a fixed [-4.5, 4.5], samples the N(0, 1) curve,
// and builds the QQ-plot points -- everything mainPlot and qqPlot need.
// The x-range is fixed so the picture doesn't jitter as n or the bin count
// changes.
setup = {
  const lo = -4.5
  const hi = 4.5
  const binCount = bins
  const binW = (hi - lo) / binCount

  const centers = new Array(binCount)
  for (let bIdx = 0; bIdx < binCount; bIdx++) centers[bIdx] = lo + (bIdx + 0.5) * binW

  const meanDensity = new Float64Array(binCount)
  const baseDensity = new Float64Array(binCount)
  const tally = (values, target) => {
    for (const v of values) {
      let idx = Math.floor((v - lo) / binW)
      if (idx < 0) idx = 0
      if (idx >= binCount) idx = binCount - 1
      target[idx]++
    }
  }
  tally(result.zMeans, meanDensity)
  tally(result.zBase, baseDensity)

  const scale = 1 / (result.M * binW)
  const meanDensityArr = new Array(binCount)
  const baseDensityArr = new Array(binCount)
  for (let bIdx = 0; bIdx < binCount; bIdx++) {
    meanDensityArr[bIdx] = meanDensity[bIdx] * scale
    baseDensityArr[bIdx] = baseDensity[bIdx] * scale
  }

  const curveXs = []
  const curveYs = []
  const steps = 220
  for (let s = 0; s <= steps; s++) {
    const x = -4.7 + 9.4 * s / steps
    curveXs.push(x)
    curveYs.push(normalPdf(x))
  }

  // The y-axis is scaled to the sample-mean histogram and the N(0, 1) peak
  // only -- NOT the n = 1 base reference. For a discrete or nearly-degenerate
  // base (rare Bernoulli, Poisson), almost every standardized single draw
  // lands in one bin, so that bar's density towers over everything; letting
  // it set the range would squash the actual comparison into a sliver. It
  // just clips off the top instead.
  let meanPeak = 0.42
  for (let bIdx = 0; bIdx < binCount; bIdx++) {
    if (meanDensityArr[bIdx] > meanPeak) meanPeak = meanDensityArr[bIdx]
  }
  const yTop = meanPeak * 1.15

  const sortedMeans = result.zMeans.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b)
  const total = sortedMeans.length
  const stride = Math.max(1, Math.floor(total / 400))
  const qq = []
  for (let i = 0; i < total; i += stride) {
    qq.push({t: normalQuantile((i + 0.5) / total), s: sortedMeans[i]})
  }

  return {
    centers,
    meanDensity: meanDensityArr,
    baseDensity: baseDensityArr,
    curveXs,
    curveYs,
    xRange: {lo: -4.7, hi: 4.7},
    yRange: {lo: 0, hi: yTop},
    qq
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
```
```{ojs}
// mainPlot: the n = 1 base histogram (behind), the standardized sample-mean
// histogram, and the N(0, 1) curve on top.
//
// _plotDiv is kept in a closure so Plotly reuses the same DOM node across
// reactive updates -- this preserves zoom and pan when n or the bin count
// changes.
mainPlot = {
  const Plotly = window.Plotly
  let _plotDiv = null

  return (data, showHist, showNormal, showBase) => {
    const traces = []
    if (showBase) {
      traces.push({x: data.centers, y: data.baseDensity, type: "bar", name: "Base distribution (n = 1)", showlegend: false, marker: {color: "#9ca3af"}, opacity: 0.45})
    }
    if (showHist) {
      traces.push({x: data.centers, y: data.meanDensity, type: "bar", name: "Sample-mean histogram", showlegend: false, marker: {color: "#2563eb"}, opacity: 0.85})
    }
    if (showNormal) {
      traces.push({x: data.curveXs, y: data.curveYs, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Normal N(0, 1)", showlegend: false, line: {color: "#dc2626", width: 3}})
    }

    const layout = {
      margin: {l: 0, r: 0, t: 0, b: 0},
      barmode: "overlay",
      bargap: 0.05,
      xaxis: {title: "standardized value", range: [data.xRange.lo, data.xRange.hi], zeroline: true},
      yaxis: {title: "density", range: [data.yRange.lo, data.yRange.hi], zeroline: true},
      hovermode: "closest",
      uirevision: "static",
      autosize: true
    }
    const config = {responsive: true, displaylogo: false}

    if (!_plotDiv) {
      _plotDiv = document.createElement("div")
      _plotDiv.className = "plotly-box-large"
      Plotly.newPlot(_plotDiv, traces, layout, config)
      // newPlot fires before the div is in the DOM, so Plotly measures 0 width.
      // A ResizeObserver catches the real size once it's inserted and laid out,
      // and keeps correcting it on any later layout/viewport change.
      new ResizeObserver(() => Plotly.Plots.resize(_plotDiv)).observe(_plotDiv)
    } else {
      Plotly.react(_plotDiv, traces, layout, config)
    }
    return _plotDiv
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
// qqPlot: a normal QQ-plot of the standardized sample means at the CURRENT
// n -- theoretical normal quantile on x, observed sample quantile on y.
// Points hug the dashed y = x line once the sample-mean distribution has
// gone normal; they bow away from it (S-shape for skew, tails off the line
// for heavy/light tails) when it hasn't.
qqPlot = {
  const line = [{x: -3.6, y: -3.6}, {x: 3.6, y: 3.6}]
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 340, height: 300, marginLeft: 46,
    x: {label: "theoretical normal quantile"},
    y: {label: "sample quantile (standardized mean)"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(line, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#9ca3af", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot(setup.qq, {x: "t", y: "s", fill: "#2563eb", r: 2})
    ]
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
// convergencePlot: how fast non-normality dies as n grows. The solid lines
// are the |skewness| and |excess kurtosis| measured from the simulated
// sample means at each n on the ladder; the dashed lines are the exact
// theoretical decays |gamma1|/sqrt(n) and |gamma2|/n for this base
// distribution. Both axes are logarithmic, so those power laws show up as
// straight lines.
convergencePlot = {
  const skewName = "|skewness| (measured)"
  const skewTheoryName = "|γ₁|/√n (exact)"
  const kurtName = "|excess kurtosis| (measured)"
  const kurtTheoryName = "|γ₂|/n (exact)"

  const floor = 1e-3
  const clampFloor = (value) => Math.max(Math.abs(value), floor)

  const skewPts = []
  const kurtPts = []
  const skewTheoryPts = []
  const kurtTheoryPts = []
  for (const row of sweep) {
    skewPts.push({n: row.n, y: clampFloor(row.skewness)})
    kurtPts.push({n: row.n, y: clampFloor(row.excessKurtosis)})
    skewTheoryPts.push({n: row.n, y: clampFloor(activeDist.skewness / Math.sqrt(row.n))})
    kurtTheoryPts.push({n: row.n, y: clampFloor(activeDist.excessKurtosis / row.n)})
  }

  const colorDomain = [skewName, skewTheoryName, kurtName, kurtTheoryName]
  const colorRange = ["#2563eb", "#2563eb", "#f59e0b", "#f59e0b"]

  const chart = Plot.plot({
    width: 340, height: 300, marginLeft: 46,
    x: {label: "sample size n", type: "log"},
    y: {label: "|standardized moment|", type: "log"},
    color: {domain: colorDomain, range: colorRange},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(skewTheoryPts, {x: "n", y: "y", stroke: () => skewTheoryName, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.lineY(kurtTheoryPts, {x: "n", y: "y", stroke: () => kurtTheoryName, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.lineY(skewPts, {x: "n", y: "y", stroke: () => skewName}),
      Plot.dot(skewPts, {x: "n", y: "y", fill: () => skewName, r: 3}),
      Plot.lineY(kurtPts, {x: "n", y: "y", stroke: () => kurtName}),
      Plot.dot(kurtPts, {x: "n", y: "y", fill: () => kurtName, r: 3})
    ]
  })
  const legend = Plot.legend({color: {domain: colorDomain, range: colorRange}})

  const container = document.createElement("div")
  container.append(chart, legend)
  return container
}
```

```{ojs}
// Convergence table -- one row per sample size on the ladder, over the
// whole simulated set (not the current n).
convergenceTable = {
  const rows = []
  for (const row of sweep) {
    rows.push([
      row.n,
      row.mean.toFixed(4),
      row.sd.toFixed(4),
      row.skewness.toFixed(4),
      row.excessKurtosis.toFixed(4),
      row.ks.toFixed(4)
    ])
  }

  return VM.ui.renderTable({
    html,
    headers: ["n", "mean", "std. dev.", "skewness", "excess kurtosis", tex`\sup_x |F_n - \Phi|`],
    csvHeaders: ["n", "mean", "std dev", "skewness", "excess kurtosis", "KS distance to N(0,1)"],
    filename: "central-limit-theorem-convergence.csv",
    rows
  })
}
```

::::

The **central limit theorem** says that for independent, identically distributed $X_1, X_2, \dots$ with finite mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, the standardized sample mean

$$
Z_n = \frac{\bar X_n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}, \qquad \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i,
$$

converges in distribution to a standard normal as $n \to \infty$ — whatever the shape of the $X_i$. That is the histogram above marching onto the red curve.

**How fast** depends on the base distribution's higher moments. The skewness and excess kurtosis of $\bar X_n$ shrink at exactly

$$
\operatorname{skew}(\bar X_n) = \frac{\gamma_1}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad
\operatorname{exkurt}(\bar X_n) = \frac{\gamma_2}{n},
$$

where $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$ are the skewness and excess kurtosis of a single $X_i$ — the dashed lines in the convergence plot. The distance to normality itself is bounded by the **Berry–Esseen theorem**,

$$
\sup_x \big| P(Z_n \le x) - \Phi(x) \big| \;\le\; \frac{C\,\rho}{\sigma^3 \sqrt{n}},
\qquad \rho = \operatorname{E}\!\big[\,|X_i - \mu|^3\,\big],
$$

with $C < 0.48$ an absolute constant. So a badly skewed or heavy-tailed base distribution (Exponential, rare Bernoulli, Log-normal) needs a much larger $n$ before $\bar X_n$ looks normal — the $1/\sqrt{n}$ rate is the same, but the constant in front is large.

The finite-variance hypothesis is not optional. Averaging draws from a **Cauchy** distribution (no finite mean, infinite variance) leaves you with the *same* Cauchy distribution for every $n$: $\bar X_n$ never concentrates and the theorem simply does not apply. Such distributions have their own limit theory built on the [stable distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution) instead.
